source.passage: Bilingual children are frequently said to enjoy a general "executive-function advantage"—better attention control and task-switching—attributed to the constant effort of managing two languages. Early studies reported such advantages, but a skeptic notes that these findings came disproportionately from small samples and were more likely to be published when the effect was positive. She hypothesizes that the reported advantage is inflated by this publication filter rather than reflecting a robust cognitive difference, and predicts a specific signature in the literature if she is right.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the skeptic's hypothesis?
choices: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.
Bilingual adults outperform monolingual adults on some attention tasks but not on others, with the gap appearing mainly on tasks that demand rapid switching.
Children who begin a second language earlier show larger executive-function advantages than those who begin later, a dose-response pattern across ages.
Monolingual children can improve their executive function through several weeks of targeted attention training.
source.key: Large, pre-registered studies find little or no bilingual advantage, while the positive results cluster among smaller studies.

adapted.passage: Many people say that children who speak two languages are better at focusing. They are also said to switch between tasks more easily. The idea is that juggling two languages trains the brain. Early studies seemed to agree. But one scientist doubts it. She points out that many of those studies were small. She also notes that a study was more likely to be published when it found an advantage. She thinks this publishing pattern made the advantage look bigger than it really is. If she is right, she says, the research should show a telltale pattern.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the scientist's idea?
choices: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.
Bilingual adults do better on some focus tasks but not others, mostly ones that need fast switching.
Children who start a second language earlier show bigger advantages than later starters.
Children who speak one language can improve their focus with weeks of special training.
adapted.key: Large, planned studies find little advantage; most positive results come from small studies.

source.passage: When a cleaner wrasse, marked with a colored spot, scraped its body against surfaces after seeing itself in a mirror, some researchers hailed the fish as self-aware, extending to it a capacity long reserved for apes and dolphins. Caution is warranted. Passing the mark test may show only that an animal can associate a mirror reflection with its own body, a sensorimotor achievement that need not involve any concept of a self. The wrasse's ecology supplies a simpler reading: a fish whose living depends on detecting blemishes on other bodies might be primed to respond to a blemish wherever a reflection places it, with no inner spectator required. To infer rich self-awareness from the behavior is to assume that one impressive performance can be produced only by the most demanding mechanism—when a leaner one, well suited to the animal's way of life, will do.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's alternative explanation of the wrasse's behavior?
choices: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.
Cleaner wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small blemishes on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Cleaner wrasses spend more time in front of a mirror than other reef fish placed in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot far more consistently than cleaner wrasses do when the same mark test is administered to both.
source.key: Wrasses try to remove marks placed on their own bodies even when the marks resemble nothing they encounter while cleaning other fish.

adapted.passage: Scientists once marked a small fish called a cleaner wrasse with a colored spot. After the fish saw itself in a mirror, it scraped its body against rocks. Some scientists said this proved the fish was self-aware, like apes and dolphins. We should be careful, though. Passing this mirror test may only show that an animal can link a reflection to its own body. That does not require any idea of a self. The wrasse's way of life gives a simpler answer. This fish gets its food by finding spots on other fish and picking them off. So it may be ready to react to a spot wherever it sees one, even in a mirror.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most weaken the author's simpler reason for what the fish does?
choices: Wrasses try to remove spots on their own bodies even when the spots look like nothing on other fish.
Wrasses are unusually quick to notice the small spots on the bodies of the fish they clean.
Wrasses spend more time looking into a mirror than other reef fish kept in the same tank do.
Apes and dolphins scrape at a marked spot much more steadily than wrasses do in the same mirror test.
adapted.key: Wrasses try to remove spots on their own bodies even when the spots look like nothing on other fish.

source.passage: The printing press is celebrated as the engine of mass literacy, as though cheaper books had straightforwardly taught Europe to read. The chronology resists the compliment. For its first century and more, print largely served readers who already existed—clergy, jurists, merchants—and the commonest products of the early presses were not primers but liturgical works and learned tomes in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. Literacy rates in many regions barely moved until the confessional campaigns and schooling drives of later centuries gave ordinary people both a reason to read and the instruction to do so. Print made those later expansions cheaper to sustain, but it did not by itself supply the motive or the teaching that literacy requires. The press was a necessary instrument of the reading public that eventually formed; it was not, on its own, the cause of that public's formation.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
choices: Across Europe the total number of books in circulation multiplied many times over within a few decades of the first printed editions.
In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.
Early printers competed fiercely for the trade in Latin editions of the classical authors.
Literacy rose fastest in the first decades after the press appeared, well before any schooling campaigns began.
source.key: In regions that adopted printing early, literacy rose sharply only generations later, once church-led schooling campaigns began.

adapted.passage: The printing press is often praised for teaching Europe to read, as if cheaper books alone made people readers. The timeline does not support that story. For more than a hundred years, printers mostly served people who could already read, such as priests, lawyers, and merchants. Most early books were church texts and scholarly works in Latin, a language most Europeans could not read at all. In many regions, reading rates barely changed until much later, when church campaigns and school programs gave ordinary people a reason to read and lessons in how to do it. Printing made those later efforts cheaper. On its own, though, it supplied neither the reason nor the teaching.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's argument?
choices: Where printing came early, reading rates rose sharply only many years later, once church schools opened.
Across Europe, the number of books grew many times over within a few short decades of the first printing.
Early printers fought hard with one another to sell Latin copies of old Greek and Roman books.
Reading rates rose fastest in the first years after printing began, well before any schools opened.
adapted.key: Where printing came early, reading rates rose sharply only many years later, once church schools opened.

source.passage: That a warming planet might make part of Europe colder sounds contradictory, yet it follows from the physics of ocean circulation. The Atlantic conveyor that carries tropical heat northward is driven partly by the sinking of cold, salty water in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it floods that region with fresh water, which is less dense and sinks less readily; the circulation slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. The claim is carefully hedged. Researchers do not predict a new ice age, nor that regional cooling would offset global warming overall—the planet keeps warming. They argue only that a global mean temperature can conceal opposing regional trends, and that a warming world is compatible with, and could even produce, a cooler northwestern Europe.
source.prompt: Which observation would most support the mechanism described in the text?
choices: Average temperatures across Europe fell even as global average temperatures rose.
As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.
Greenland's ice sheet lost mass more rapidly during warmer years, shedding meltwater from its margins at rates that tracked each summer's temperatures.
Tropical ocean temperatures rose in step with the global average temperature.
source.key: As freshwater flowing into the North Atlantic increased, the sinking of deep water slowed and the northward transport of heat weakened.

adapted.passage: It sounds strange that a warming planet could make part of Europe colder, but the ocean explains how. A huge Atlantic current carries warm water from the tropics north toward Europe. The current is driven partly by cold, salty water sinking in the far North Atlantic. As Greenland's ice melts, it pours fresh water into that area. Fresh water is lighter, so it does not sink as easily. The current then slows, and less tropical heat reaches northwestern Europe. Scientists are careful about this claim. They do not predict a new ice age, and they agree that the planet as a whole keeps warming. They say only that a warmer world could still produce a cooler northwestern Europe.
adapted.prompt: Which observation would most support the process described in the passage?
choices: As more fresh water flowed into the North Atlantic, deep water sank more slowly and less heat moved north.
Across all of Europe, it got colder even as the world as a whole got warmer.
Greenland's ice sheet lost ice faster in warmer years, and more of it melted off its edges during each hot summer.
Ocean water in the tropics warmed at the same pace as the world as a whole did.
adapted.key: As more fresh water flowed into the North Atlantic, deep water sank more slowly and less heat moved north.

source.passage: Standard narratives attribute Japan's swift industrialization after 1868 to the Meiji government's importation of Western machinery and foreign advisers. The hardware mattered, but it does not explain why Japan absorbed what other nineteenth-century states could not. Long before Commodore Perry, Tokugawa Japan possessed high literacy, a dense commercial network, sophisticated rural proto-industry, and merchant houses skilled in double-entry accounting and futures trading. These endowments meant that imported technology met a workforce and a managerial class already primed to deploy it. Foreign experts were, tellingly, dismissed as soon as Japanese personnel could replace them—often within a decade. The Meiji reformers' genuine innovation lay less in acquiring foreign techniques than in redirecting indigenous capacities toward national ends. Where historians once read the period as a story of borrowing, the more defensible reading treats borrowing as the visible surface of a deeper continuity, one that the drama of Westernization has tended to obscure.
source.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's central claim?
choices: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machinery than any other contemporaneous Asian state.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid substantially higher salaries than they had earned at home, a premium that drew engineers and accountants to Meiji ministries.
Tokugawa-era literacy rates were significantly lower in rural regions than in major cities.
source.key: A neighboring state that imported identical Western machinery but lacked comparable commercial institutions failed to industrialize at a similar pace.

adapted.passage: Most histories say Japan built factories quickly after 1868 for one reason. Its new Meiji government brought in Western machines and foreign advisers. The machines mattered, but they do not explain why Japan could put them to use when many other countries could not. Long before 1868, Japan already had high literacy, busy trade networks, and skilled village workshops. Its merchant houses kept careful account books. So the new machines met workers and managers who were ready to run them. Foreign experts were sent home as soon as Japanese workers could replace them, often within ten years. Japan's success came less from borrowing than from business skills it already had.
adapted.prompt: Which finding, if true, would most strengthen the author's main claim?
choices: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.
The Meiji government spent more on foreign machines than any other country in Asia did then.
Foreign advisers in Japan were paid much more than they had earned at home, a bonus that drew many engineers.
Before 1868, reading rates in Japan's country villages were much lower than in its large cities.
adapted.key: A nearby country that bought the same machines but lacked those business skills built factories more slowly.

source.passage: The 'hygiene hypothesis' is popularly summarized as a simple warning: modern cleanliness, by depriving children of germs, leaves their immune systems untrained and prone to allergy. Immunologists have largely abandoned that formulation. The rise in allergic disease does not correlate well with reduced exposure to the common infectious agents of childhood—colds, flus, and the like—which the crude version implicates. It correlates instead with diminished contact with a particular set of ancient, largely harmless microorganisms, the so-called 'old friends' that co-evolved with humans and help calibrate immune regulation. On this refined account, the problem is not insufficient infection but the loss of specific symbiotic exposures; a childhood full of ordinary colds confers little protection, while contact with the right environmental microbes does. Cleanliness is not quite the villain the slogan suggests.
source.prompt: Which finding would most directly support the refined account over the popular version of the hygiene hypothesis?
choices: Children raised in unusually clean, nearly germ-free households had markedly higher rates of allergic disease than did children who grew up in ordinary, less sanitized homes.
Adults who contract frequent respiratory infections tend to have weaker immune systems overall than adults who rarely fall ill.
Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.
The 'old friend' microorganisms were far more common in the human environments of thousands of years ago than they are in the households of modern industrialized countries today.
source.key: Children who suffered many ordinary childhood infections were no less allergic than those who suffered few, whereas children exposed to diverse environmental microbes were.

adapted.passage: The "hygiene hypothesis" is often told as a simple warning. Modern homes are so clean that children meet few germs. As a result, their immune systems never learn properly, and allergies follow. Most immune scientists no longer accept that version. The rise in allergies does not match up well with fewer common childhood illnesses, such as colds and flu. Instead, it matches up with less contact with certain ancient, mostly harmless microbes. These "old friends" evolved alongside humans and help tune the immune system. In this newer view, a childhood full of colds gives little protection, while contact with the right microbes from the environment does.
adapted.prompt: Which finding would best support the newer view rather than the popular version?
choices: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.
Children raised in very clean homes with almost no germs had far more allergies than children from less clean homes.
Adults who often catch colds and flu tend to have weaker immune systems than adults who rarely get sick.
The "old friend" microbes were far more common in human homes thousands of years ago than in homes today.
adapted.key: Children with many colds were no less allergic than those with few, but children living near varied microbes were.
